node.label: Indigenous–newcomer relations & fur-trade history
node.period_rationale: Period 2 (c. 1970–85) is when the field takes shape: Ray 1974, Trigger 1976 and 1985, Van Kirk and Brown 1980, Delâge 1985. Innis 1930 and Stanley 1936 are earlier resources, not origins; syntheses, schools, health and labour studies continue through period 3.
node.date_label: Earlier resources: Innis 1930, Stanley 1936 · Ray 1974 · Van Kirk and Brown 1980 · Trigger’s Natives and Newcomers 1985 · Miller 1989 · Milloy 1999 · coverage through 2000, selected later works

date_span.basis: Selected publication milestones. 1930 and 1936 are earlier works the field reworks, not its origin; 1974–85 is the field’s formation; 2000 is the atlas coverage boundary, not an end.

node.description: A Canadian historiography of relations between Indigenous peoples and European newcomers, centred first on the fur trade and then on policy, schools, missions, health and labour. Innis’s Fur Trade in Canada (1930) was subtitled ‘an introduction to Canadian economic history’. From the 1970s historians, geographers and archaeologists recast it with Indigenous people as actors: trappers, hunters and middlemen (Ray 1974), wives and kin in fur-trade society (Van Kirk; Brown, both 1980), and Wendat history across contact (Trigger 1976, 1985; Delâge 1985), while Dickason studied European representations of them (1984). The field long called itself ‘native–newcomer’ history, after Trigger’s Natives and Newcomers (1985); current usage prefers ‘Indigenous’. Miller (1989) offered a national synthesis of ‘Indian–white relations’. Later work studied reserve farming and policy (Carter 1990), residential schools (Miller 1996; Milloy 1999), health (Kelm 1998) and wage labour (Lutz 1992). Brownlie and Kelm (1994) asked whether agency-centred work on Indian policy and the potlatch law (Cole and Chaikin; Miller; Loo) had made Native agency a colonialist alibi. Indigenous scholars questioned the framing: Sioui (1989) found conventional history without a method for Indigenous self-interpretation; Winona Stevenson (Wheeler) (1998) argued that historians of ‘Indian–White relations’, relying on one side’s records, kept even agency-centred work within a colonialist framework and set oral history aside; LaRocque (1999) found that the cross-cultural ethnohistory of Trigger, Brown and Van Kirk still ‘othered’ its subjects. After 2000, settler-colonial analysis read this history as continuing dispossession; Greer replied that the fur trade’s commercial penetration was a different form of invasion.
node.scope_note: A research field in mostly academic, mostly non-Indigenous Canadian historiography, built on company, church and state archives together with archaeology and anthropology. It is not the atlas’s Indigenous history entry, which centres Indigenous historical traditions, community knowledge and authority. Several people sit in both (Dickason, Miller, Lutz, Trigger); their existing contexts are kept, and Indigenous historical practice is not subsumed here. It is not Settler colonialism, which reads dispossession as a continuing structure: most works here predate that framework and do not adopt it, and Greer’s critique points the other way. Indigenous critiques of the ‘relations’ framing (Sioui, LaRocque; Fixico and S. Miller in the US) appear as critics, not members, and the roster records no identity classification. Francophone work is thin in this selection (Delâge, Sioui); New France encounter history overlaps with Quebec historiography. The label keeps the field’s word ‘newcomer’ but uses ‘Indigenous’; ‘native–newcomer’, Trigger’s 1985 term, is explained in the description as the field’s historical name. ‘Indigenous–settler’ is avoided so as not to collide with settler_colonialism.

strands.title: The fur trade in national history
strands.focus: Innis makes the fur trade an introduction to Canadian economic history (1930); Stanley’s history of the West and the Riel resistances (1936) is reprinted and cited for decades. Both are resources the field later reworks, not its founders.
strands.works: Innis, The Fur Trade in Canada (1930); Stanley, The Birth of Western Canada (1936)

strands.title: Indigenous people as actors in the trade
strands.focus: Ray reconstructs Indigenous people’s roles as trappers, hunters and middlemen (1974); Fisher writes British Columbia contact as Indian–European relations (1977).
strands.works: Ray, Indians in the Fur Trade (1974); Fisher, Contact and Conflict (1977)

strands.title: Fur-trade families, Métis peoples and voyageurs
strands.focus: Women and kinship (Van Kirk) and company families (Brown) recast fur-trade society in 1980; Peterson and Brown’s collection treats Métis peoples in their own right (1985). Podruchny (2006) and Macdougall (2010) carry the strand into the extension.
strands.works: Van Kirk (1980); Brown (1980); Peterson and Brown, eds. (1985); Podruchny (2006); Macdougall (2010)

strands.title: Contact, the Wendat and European representations
strands.focus: Trigger joins archaeology and documents to Wendat/Huron history before and after contact (1976) and reconsiders the ‘heroic age’ of New France (1985). Delâge writes the same encounter in French (1985); Dickason studies European representations (1984). Shared with the Ethnohistory entry.
strands.works: Trigger, The Children of Aataentsic (1976), Natives and Newcomers (1985); Delâge, Le pays renversé (1985); Dickason, The Myth of the Savage (1984)

strands.title: How historians wrote about Indigenous peoples
strands.focus: Walker (1971) and Trigger (1986) survey Canadian historical writing about Indigenous peoples. Trigger dates such studies from 1971 and describes ethnohistorical work across disciplines moving into national history.
strands.works: Walker, “The Indian in Canadian Historical Writing” (1971); Trigger, “The Historians’ Indian” (1986)

strands.title: Syntheses of relations and policy
strands.focus: Miller’s national synthesis of ‘Indian–white relations’ (1989), Dickason’s history of First Nations (1992), and regional or biographical studies (Smith 1987; Coates 1991). Miller’s and Dickason’s books differ in authorship and standpoint; they are grouped here as syntheses, not as one interpretation.
strands.works: Smith, Sacred Feathers (1987); Miller, Skyscrapers Hide the Heavens (1989); Coates, Best Left as Indians (1991); Dickason, Canada’s First Nations (1992)

strands.title: Reserves, residential schools and Indian agents
strands.focus: Reserve agriculture and policy (Carter 1990), residential schools (Miller 1996; Milloy 1999) and Indian agents (Brownlie 2003). These studies predate the settler-colonial framework and do not adopt it.
strands.works: Carter, Lost Harvests (1990); Miller, Shingwauk’s Vision (1996); Milloy, “A National Crime” (1999); Brownlie, A Fatherly Eye (2003)

strands.title: Health, missions and authenticity
strands.focus: Kelm reads health and healing through the body and colonial power (1998); Rutherdale studies gender and race in the mission field (2002); Raibmon treats authenticity as made by unequal collaborators (2005).
strands.works: Kelm, Colonizing Bodies (1998); Rutherdale, Women and the White Man’s God (2002); Raibmon, Authentic Indians (2005)

strands.title: Indigenous labour after the fur trade
strands.focus: Lutz treats Aboriginal people in British Columbia as a labouring class (1992) and later rewrites Aboriginal–white relations (2008). This is the strand that meets Canadian working-class history.

strands.title: Agency as alibi? An internal critique
strands.focus: Brownlie and Kelm (1994) criticised agency-centred work on Indian policy and the potlatch law (Cole and Chaikin 1990; Miller; Loo 1992): stressing Native agency exaggerated how far it became effective self-defence, trivialising the harm of colonial policy and serving as an ‘alibi’ for it. A critique within policy history, not of the fur-trade literature; targets known from a secondary source, essay unread.
strands.works: Robin Brownlie and Mary-Ellen Kelm, “Desperately Seeking Absolution: Native Agency as Colonialist Alibi?” CHR 75:4 (December 1994): 543–56

strands.title: Indigenous critiques of the relations frame
strands.focus: Sioui (1989), Stevenson/Wheeler (1998) and LaRocque (1999) criticise the relations framing from Indigenous standpoints: its reliance on colonial documents, its disregard of oral history and its ethnological distance. Fixico and S. Miller (2009, US) question ‘Indian–white relations’ as the premise of Indian history. Paul’s We Were Not the Savages (1993; the 2000 Fernwood edition is the one PhDs cite), subtitled ‘a Mi’kmaq perspective’, rejects the ‘savage’ category (title and subtitle only). Adams’s Prison of Grass (1975) is an earlier counter-history of official history, not a critique of this field, and Dickason is a member of the field. Trigger (1986) and Brownlie and Kelm (1994) are non-Indigenous critiques from inside. These are critics and alternatives, not members.
strands.works: Sioui (1989); Paul (1993; 2000 ed.); Stevenson [Wheeler] (Fall 1998); LaRocque (1999); Fixico (2009); S. A. Miller (2009)

strands.title: After 2000: the settler-colonial reading and its critics
strands.focus: Settler-colonial analysis reads reserves, schools and dispossession as a continuing structure. Greer replies that the settler mode dominates some periods and regions and fades in others, and that commercial penetration (the fur trade’s mode) and extractivism are other forms of invasion. Konishi records Indigenous scholars’ critiques of settler colonial studies. Extension only.

extension_coverage.note: Selected post-2000 works only; the field continues. The settler-colonial reading is the separate proposed entry.

relation_to_periods: Main-period entry. Formation in period 2 (1974–85), consolidation in period 3; Innis 1930 and Stanley 1936 are earlier resources. Post-2000 works (Rutherdale 2002, Brownlie 2003, Raibmon 2005, Podruchny 2006, Lutz 2008, Macdougall 2010, and the 2009 US critiques) are selected extension records, not a complete review.

proposed_relationships.relationship: Ethnohistorical method in Canadian native–newcomer history
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: Trigger’s Wendat/Huron history joins archaeology, ethnography and contact records (existing atlas source), and his 1986 survey describes historians, anthropologists, archaeologists, geographers and economists combining in ethnohistorical research that was being integrated into national history. Bruce Trigger is already on the Ethnohistory roster; this edge records a contribution, not a founding claim.

Overlapping subjects and people (Dickason, Miller, Lutz), different centres: Indigenous history centres Indigenous historical authority; this field centres relations, policy and encounter, often from colonial archives. The Indigenous entry’s existing strand native_newcomer_institutions (Miller) is the in-atlas meeting point. Comparison only: neither field is a subset of the other.

proposed_relationships.relationship: Indigenous critiques of the relations frame
proposed_relationships.map_label: Indigenous critiques: autohistory, othering and colonizing practices
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: Sioui proposes autohistory: Indigenous self-interpretation and transmitted traditions in historical discourse (interview, 1991). Winona Stevenson (Wheeler) (Saskatchewan History, Fall 1998; read in full) argues that historians of ‘Indian–White relations’, relying on one side’s records, keep even agency-centred work within a colonialist framework. LaRocque’s 1999 dissertation criticises the ‘neo cross-cultural approach’ of Trigger, Brown, Van Kirk and others as still othering (PDF pp. 249, 102, 109, 30 n.). Fixico (2009, US) says the premise of ‘Indian–white relations’ must be turned over for an Indian point of view. Fixico and S. Miller write about US historiography; they are cited as parallel critiques, not as statements about the Canadian books listed here. No identity classification is recorded.

proposed_relationships.relationship: Relations and encounter versus a structure of dispossession
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: The same archives and subjects (reserves, schools, policy) are read as relations and encounter here and as a continuing settler structure in the proposed Settler colonialism entry. Greer argues the settler mode dominates some periods and regions and fades in others; commercial penetration, the fur-trade mode, is another. Most native–newcomer works predate the settler framework and do not adopt it. PhD context: among 2009–2026 PhDs engaging this roster (two or more people cited), the share also citing Wolfe’s or Veracini’s settler-colonial works rises from 1 of 66 (2009–14) to 14 of 88 (2015–19) and 26 of 65 (2020–26), while engagement with the roster holds steady (16.1% → 16.0% of all PhDs). Bibliographies record consultation, not adoption.

proposed_relationships.relationship: Innis’s fur trade as a resource reworked by later historians
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: Innis made the fur trade an introduction to Canadian economic history (1930). Ray’s later reconstruction of Indigenous traders reorients that subject; a later UTP reissue of Innis carries Ray’s credit (catalogue only). Contribution of a subject and evidence base, not influence on the field’s interpretations. PhD context: Innis is cited by 82 PhDs, The Fur Trade in Canada by 48.

proposed_relationships.relationship: Aboriginal people as a labouring class
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: Lutz’s “After the Fur Trade: The Aboriginal Labouring Class of British Columbia” (1992) brings Indigenous wage and exchange labour into working-class history. One specific intervention; Canadian labour historians are not assumed to have adopted it. Distinct from the settler packet’s Burrill (2019) edge, which proposes a settler-order framework for the same field.

proposed_relationships.relationship: Gender, marriage and missions in fur-trade and colonial society
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: Van Kirk’s women in fur-trade society (1980) and Rutherdale’s gender and race in the mission field (2002) belong to both fields; Van Kirk also anchors the proposed women and gender entry. Comparison, no direction asserted.

Kelm’s publisher description reads health and healing through postcolonial conceptions of the body and the power relations of colonization, as ethnohistory. A specific overlap with the Medical & health history entry; optional.

relationships_considered_not_proposed.reason: Delâge, Sioui and Trigger write New France encounter history, and 47 PhDs engage both rosters (lift 1.74), but no checked source states the connection. A lead for the Quebec drafter.
Carter and Fisher are also regional (Prairie, British Columbia) historians; rosters are not edges and no checked work frames the link.
Kelm’s postcolonial framing and Trigger’s anthropology are already carried by the ethnohistory and medicalhistory proposals.
No checked settler-colonial work criticises native–newcomer history by name; Regan’s ‘peacemaker myth’ targets national narratives (settler packet edge 4). Kept as a comparison.

open_questions: Label: keep “Native–newcomer”, Trigger’s 1985 term, as a historical name for the field, or use “Indigenous–settler relations” as the label with “native–newcomer” in the description? The older term is what the historiography called itself; current usage prefers Indigenous.
Roster is 22 (above the brief’s 8–20) because all 16 groups.json primary people are kept and Delâge, Fisher, Sioui and LaRocque are added. Drop Fisher or move Sioui and LaRocque to strands only?

Indigenous critique: Sioui and LaRocque are Canadian and already in the atlas; Fixico and S. A. Miller are US. Is a Canadian Indigenous critique of the fur-trade/relations framing before 2000 available (e.g. Winona Wheeler’s work, which could not be verified here)?
Kelm and Brownlie (1994) is attested by title only (MUSE blocks automated access). Which books does it review? Check before using it beyond the title.
Innis: his primary placement is cdn_national_tradition. Confirm he is a precursor here, and whether the cdn_national_tradition → native_newcomer contribution edge is wanted.
Daniel N. Paul (1993) is cited at title level only. Keep it as a witness to an Indigenous-authored counter-history, or drop it until the book is checked?
